title: Generative machine learning nominates a chiral ligand validated in asymmetric C–H activation
summary: A transfer-learned chemical language model generated novel chiral amino-acid ligands for palladium-catalyzed asymmetric β-C(sp³)–H activation, while an ensemble of 30 fine-tuned deep-learning regressors predicted reaction enantioselectivity. From 490 generated ligand candidates, mechanistic and synthetic filters retained 73; the authors tested selected reactions prospectively without disclosing the model-predicted enantioselectivity to the experimentalists. One highlighted reaction using generated ligand L5 gave 94% ee, matching the model prediction of 94%.
ai_technology: Transfer-learned ULMFiT chemical language model (FnG) for ligand generation and a 30-model deep-learning ensemble (EnP) for enantioselectivity prediction
organization: Indian Institute of Technology Bombay; Scripps Research

evidence.tested: From 490 generated ligand candidates, mechanistic and synthetic filters retained 73; the authors tested selected reactions prospectively without disclosing the model-predicted enantioselectivity to the experimentalists. The coauthor collaboration tested newly generated candidates; blinding experimentalists to model predictions is distinct from independent follow-up replication.
evidence.unknown: The accepted manuscript reports proof-of-concept prospective chemistry rather than a broadly validated catalyst family: only a small, expert-selected subset was tested and the authors report that some generated ligands were infeasible or failed to form product. The highlighted result is a ligand for an established C–H activation reaction, not a new reaction class; it does not establish scale-up or utility beyond tested conditions. The selected reaction gave 94% ee, but the accessible text table names it L5 and summarizes substrate/coupling partner graphically rather than in searchable prose.
evidence.ai_role: FnG generated candidate chiral ligands from a model fine-tuned on known ligands, while EnP ranked reactions formed by pairing generated ligands with known substrates/coupling partners. The researchers selected a small set for blinded prospective wet-lab testing; the paper reports one highlighted new ligand/reaction at 94% ee, matching prediction.
